```go
package cli

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"

	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/catalog"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/config"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/gitx"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/pathx"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/repo"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/tui"
)

func setRepositoryFavorite(ctx context.Context, app *App, row tui.RepoRow, desired bool) (*catalog.Entry, error) {
	if app == nil || app.Registry == nil {
		return nil, errors.New("repository catalog is unavailable")
	}
	if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	id := ""
	if row.Asset != nil {
		id = row.Asset.ID
	}
	if id == "" {
		path, err := repo.ValidateNavigation(ctx, row.Repo, "")
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		realPath, err := pathx.Canonical(path)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		observation := catalog.Observation{Host: config.Hostname(), Path: path, RealPath: realPath, Name: row.Repo.Name}
		if row.Repo.HasGit || row.Repo.CommonDir != "" || row.Repo.GitDir != "" {
			git, err := gitx.Discover(ctx, path)
			if err != nil {
				return nil, fmt.Errorf("validate favorite repository: %w", err)
			}
			observation.CommonDir = git.GitCommonDir
			observation.RemoteIdentity = gitx.RemoteFromConfig(git.GitCommonDir, "origin")
		}
		entry, err := app.Registry.EnsureRepository(observation)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		id = entry.ID
	}
	// The preference belongs to the stable asset, not the current availability
	// of its checkout. In particular a missing favorite can still be removed.
	return app.Registry.Patch(id, func(entry *catalog.Entry) error {
		if entry.Kind != catalog.KindRepository {
			return errors.New("favorites are only available for repositories")
		}
		entry.Favorite = desired
		return nil
	})
}
```

```go
package cli

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"time"

	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/diskusage"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/forge"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/gitx"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/inventory"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/note"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/runtime"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/task"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/tui"
)

// prepareRepoRowCollector reads shared inputs once. Admission and the shared
// limiter belong to callers, not to one goroutine per repository.
func prepareRepoRowCollector(ctx context.Context, app *App, rt runtime.Runtime, options repoCollectOptions) (func(context.Context, tui.RepoRow) tui.RepoRow, error) {
	tasks := options.Tasks
	var taskInventoryErr error
	if !options.TasksSet {
		var diagnostics []task.Diagnostic
		var err error
		tasks, diagnostics, err = app.Tasks.ListWithDiagnostics()
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		for _, diagnostic := range diagnostics {
			taskInventoryErr = errors.Join(taskInventoryErr, diagnostic)
		}
	}
	byRepo := map[string][]*task.Task{}
	for _, tracked := range tasks {
		byRepo[tracked.RepoPath] = append(byRepo[tracked.RepoPath], tracked)
	}
	sessions, runtimeErr := options.Sessions, options.SessionsErr
	if !options.SessionsSet {
		sessions, runtimeErr = rt.List(ctx)
	}
	notesByRepo := map[string][]*note.Note{}
	if app.Notes != nil {
		allNotes, err := app.Notes.List("")
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		for _, n := range allNotes {
			notesByRepo[n.RepositoryID] = append(notesByRepo[n.RepositoryID], n)
		}
	}
	return func(ctx context.Context, row tui.RepoRow) tui.RepoRow {
		r := row.Repo
		row.ObservedAt = time.Now()
		if row.Asset != nil {
			repoNotes := notesByRepo[row.Asset.ID]
			row.NoteCount = len(repoNotes)
			if len(repoNotes) > 0 {
				row.LatestNote = repoNotes[0]
			}
		}
		if r.HasGit {
			if options.DeferTopology {
				row.TopologyPending = true
				row.TopologyErr = errors.New("recovery details not loaded")
			} else {
				row.Topology, row.TopologyErr = gitx.RecoveryTopologyOf(ctx, r.Path)
			}
		}
		row.Tasks = append(row.Tasks, byRepo[r.Path]...)
		if r.RealPath != "" && r.RealPath != r.Path {
			row.Tasks = append(row.Tasks, byRepo[r.RealPath]...)
		}
		row.Context = inventory.CollectRepoContext(ctx, r, row.Tasks, sessions, rt.Name())
		row.Context.TaskErr = taskInventoryErr
		row.Context.RuntimeErr = runtimeErr
		row.LastActivity, row.Worktrees = row.Context.LastActivity, row.Context.WorktreeCount
		if main, ok := row.Context.Main(); ok {
			row.Status, row.GitKnown = main.Status, main.StatusErr == nil
		}
		if !r.Bare {
			row.RemoteForge, row.RemoteName = forge.IdentityFromURL(gitx.RemoteFromConfig(r.CommonDir, "origin"))
		}
		if live := row.Context.Sessions(); len(live) > 0 {
			row.Live, row.Runtime = true, rt.Name()
			row.RuntimeHandle, row.RuntimeStatus = live[0].Handle, live[0].AgentStatus
		}
		if r.HasGit {
			row.SizeTarget = diskusage.FromGit(gitx.Repo{
				Root: r.Path, GitDir: r.GitDir, GitCommonDir: r.CommonDir,
				MainRoot: r.MainRoot, Name: r.Name, Bare: r.Bare,
			}, row.Worktrees)
		} else {
			row.SizeTarget = diskusage.Plain(r.Path)
		}
		return row
	}, nil
}
```

```text
13	// Repo identifies one repository, independent of which worktree you are
14	// standing in. Two linked worktrees of the same clone share a Key.
15	type Repo struct {
16		// Root is the working-tree root of the checkout that was probed.
17		Root string
18		// GitDir is this checkout's administrative directory. A linked worktree has
19		// its own entry below the shared common directory.
20		GitDir string
21		// GitCommonDir is the shared .git directory — the same value for every
22		// worktree of a clone, which makes it the natural identity.
23		GitCommonDir string
24		// Name is the basename users recognise the repo by.
25		Name string
26		// IsLinkedWorktree reports whether Root is a linked worktree rather than
27		// the main checkout.
28		IsLinkedWorktree bool
29		// MainRoot is the main (non-linked) checkout of this clone.
30		MainRoot string
31		// Bare reports whether the main checkout is a bare repository.
32		Bare bool
33	}

35	// Key is the stable identity of the clone, shared by all its worktrees.
36	func (r Repo) Key() string { return r.GitCommonDir }

38	// Discover probes dir and reports the repository containing it.
39	func Discover(ctx context.Context, dir string) (Repo, error) {
40		// A single rev-parse call answers everything: batching avoids four
41		// process spawns per repo, which matters when scanning 39 of them.
42		out, err := run(ctx, dir,
43			"rev-parse",
44			"--path-format=absolute",
45			"--show-toplevel",
46			"--git-dir",
47			"--git-common-dir",
48			"--is-bare-repository",
49		)
50		if err != nil {
51			return Repo{}, err
52		}
53		f := lines(out)
54		r := Repo{}
55		// A bare repo has no toplevel, so git prints one fewer line.
56		switch len(f) {
57		case 4:
58			r.Root = f[0]
59			r.GitDir = f[1]
60			r.GitCommonDir = f[2]
61			r.Bare = f[3] == "true"
62		case 3:
63			r.GitDir = f[0]
64			r.GitCommonDir = f[1]
65			r.Bare = f[2] == "true"
66		default:
67			return Repo{}, ErrNotARepo
68		}
69	
70		// Git for Windows reports forward slashes and may expand an 8.3 path.
71		// Expose one physical, native spelling at the Git boundary so callers never
72		// compare those strings with an unrelated lexical spelling of the same path.
73		for _, field := range []*string{&r.Root, &r.GitDir, &r.GitCommonDir} {
74			if *field == "" {
75				continue
76			}
77			*field, err = pathx.Canonical(*field)
78			if err != nil {
79				return Repo{}, fmt.Errorf("canonicalize Git repository path: %w", err)
80			}
81		}
82	
83		// The main checkout is the parent of the common .git dir, except for a
84		// bare repo (where the common dir *is* the repo).
85		if r.Bare {
86			r.MainRoot = strings.TrimSuffix(r.GitCommonDir, string(filepath.Separator))
87		} else if r.GitDir == r.GitCommonDir {
88			// A normal checkout may use --separate-git-dir, so the common directory's
89			// parent is not necessarily the working-tree root.
90			r.MainRoot = r.Root
91		} else {
92			r.MainRoot = filepath.Dir(r.GitCommonDir)
93			// Absorbed submodules keep their repository below the superproject's
94			// modules directory. Its parent is metadata, not a checkout.
95			if configured, configErr := run(ctx, dir, "config", "--file", filepath.Join(r.GitCommonDir, "config"), "--get", "core.worktree"); configErr == nil && configured != "" {
96				if !filepath.IsAbs(configured) {
97					configured = filepath.Join(r.GitCommonDir, configured)
98				}
99				r.MainRoot = filepath.Clean(configured)
100			}
101			probe, probeErr := run(ctx, r.MainRoot, "rev-parse", "--path-format=absolute", "--show-toplevel", "--git-common-dir")
102			fields := lines(probe)
103			if probeErr != nil || len(fields) != 2 || !sameCanonicalPath(fields[1], r.GitCommonDir) {
104				return Repo{}, fmt.Errorf("cannot verify main checkout for Git common directory %s", r.GitCommonDir)
105			}
106			r.MainRoot, err = pathx.Canonical(fields[0])
107			if err != nil {
108				return Repo{}, fmt.Errorf("canonicalize main checkout: %w", err)
109			}
110		}
111		r.IsLinkedWorktree = r.Root != "" && r.GitDir != r.GitCommonDir
112		r.Name = filepath.Base(r.MainRoot)
113		if r.Bare {
114			// ".../foo/.bare" or ".../foo.git" should both read as "foo".
115			r.Name = strings.TrimSuffix(filepath.Base(r.MainRoot), ".git")
116			if strings.HasPrefix(r.Name, ".") {
117				r.Name = filepath.Base(filepath.Dir(r.MainRoot))
118			}
119		}
120		return r, nil
121	}

127		return err == nil
```

```go
package cli

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"path/filepath"
	"strings"

	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/catalog"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/gitx"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/repo"
	"github.com/daviddwlee84/dev-cli/internal/tui"
)

// Preferences are read from the durable catalog, never from the observation
// cache. This snapshot is read-only and scoped to one load generation.
type tuiRepoCatalog struct {
	entries []*catalog.Entry
	seeds   []tui.RepoRow
	host    string
}

func readTUIRepoCatalog(ctx context.Context, app *App) (tuiRepoCatalog, error) {
	out := tuiRepoCatalog{host: configHostname()}
	if app.Catalog == nil {
		return out, nil
	}
	entries, diagnostics, err := app.Catalog.ListWithDiagnostics()
	if err != nil {
		return out, fmt.Errorf("catalog metadata: %w", err)
	}
	out.entries = entries
	for _, diagnostic := range diagnostics {
		err = errors.Join(err, diagnostic)
	}
	for _, entry := range entries {
		if ctx.Err() != nil {
			return out, errors.Join(err, ctx.Err())
		}
		if !entry.Favorite || entry.Kind != catalog.KindRepository {
			continue
		}
		location, ok := entry.LocationFor(out.host)
		if !ok || location.CurrentPath == "" {
			continue
		}
		for _, root := range app.Cfg.DiscoveryRoots() {
			covered, scopeErr := repo.PathDiscoverableFromRoot(root, location.CurrentPath, repo.DefaultOptions())
			if scopeErr != nil {
				err = errors.Join(err, fmt.Errorf("favorite %s discovery scope: %w", entry.Title(), scopeErr))
				continue
			}
			if !covered {
				continue
			}
			category := ""
			if relative, relErr := filepath.Rel(root, location.CurrentPath); relErr == nil && relative != ".." && !strings.HasPrefix(relative, ".."+string(filepath.Separator)) {
				category = filepath.ToSlash(filepath.Dir(relative))
				if category == "." {
					category = ""
				}
			}
			out.seeds = append(out.seeds, tui.RepoRow{
				Repo: repo.Repo{Name: filepath.Base(location.CurrentPath), Path: location.CurrentPath,
					RealPath: location.RealPath, CommonDir: location.GitCommonDir,
					Root: root, Category: category, HasGit: location.GitCommonDir != ""},
				Asset: entry.Clone(), Pending: "loading",
			})
			break
		}
	}
	return out, err
}

func (c tuiRepoCatalog) asset(repository repo.Repo) *catalog.Entry {
	var match *catalog.Entry
	for _, entry := range c.entries {
		location, ok := entry.LocationFor(c.host)
		if !ok || location.State != catalog.LocationPresent || !repoLocationMatches(repository, location) {
			continue
		}
		if match != nil {
			// Ambiguous metadata must not acquire authority through discovery.
			return nil
		}
		match = entry
	}
	if match == nil {
		return nil
	}
	return match.Clone()
}

func discoverTUIFavorite(ctx context.Context, expected repo.Repo) (repo.Repo, error) {
	if _, err := repo.ValidateNavigation(ctx, expected, expected.Path); err != nil {
		return expected, err
	}
	g, err := gitx.Discover(ctx, expected.Path)
	if err != nil {
		if !expected.HasGit && errors.Is(err, gitx.ErrNotARepo) {
			expected.RealPath = canonicalRepoValue(expected.Path)
			return expected, nil
		}
		return expected, err
	}
	if g.IsLinkedWorktree {
		return expected, errors.New("favorite target is a linked worktree, not a repository root")
	}
	expected.RealPath, expected.GitDir, expected.CommonDir = g.MainRoot, g.GitDir, g.GitCommonDir
	expected.MainRoot, expected.HasGit, expected.Bare = g.MainRoot, true, g.Bare
	expected.Symlink = filepath.Clean(expected.Path) != expected.RealPath
	return expected, nil
}

// Keys use physical paths and Git common directories, never display names.
// Seed keys reserve only potentially matching work until target validation;
// only freshly validated keys authorize deduplication of enrichment.
func tuiRepoKeys(r repo.Repo) []string {
	var keys []string
	if common := canonicalRepoValue(r.CommonDir); common != "" {
		keys = append(keys, "git:"+common)
	}
	for path := range canonicalRepoValues(r.Path, r.RealPath) {
		keys = append(keys, "path:"+path)
	}
	return keys
}
```

A skill for creating new skills and iteratively improving them.

At a high level, the process of creating a skill goes like this:

- Decide what you want the skill to do and roughly how it should do it

- Create a few test prompts and run claude-with-access-to-the-skill on them
- Help the user evaluate the results both qualitatively and quantitatively
  - While the runs happen in the background, draft some quantitative evals if there aren't any (if there are some, you can either use as is or modify if you feel something needs to change about them). Then explain them to the user (or if they already existed, explain the ones that already exist)
  - Use the `eval-viewer/generate_review.py` script to show the user the results for them to look at, and also let them look at the quantitative metrics
- Rewrite the skill based on feedback from the user's evaluation of the results (and also if there are any glaring flaws that become apparent from the quantitative benchmarks)
- Repeat until you're satisfied
- Expand the test set and try again at larger scale

Your job when using this skill is to figure out where the user is in this process and then jump in and help them progress through these stages. So for instance, maybe they're like "I want to make a skill for X". You can help narrow down what they mean, write a draft, write the test cases, figure out how they want to evaluate, run all the prompts, and repeat.

On the other hand, maybe they already have a draft of the skill. In this case you can go straight to the eval/iterate part of the loop.

Of course, you should always be flexible and if the user is like "I don't need to run a bunch of evaluations, just vibe with me", you can do that instead.

Then after the skill is done (but again, the order is flexible), you can also run the skill description improver, which we have a whole separate script for, to optimize the triggering of the skill.

Cool? Cool.

## Communicating with the user

The skill creator is liable to be used by people across a wide range of familiarity with coding jargon. If you haven't heard (and how could you, it's only very recently that it started), there's a trend now where the power of Claude is inspiring plumbers to open up their terminals, parents and grandparents to google "how to install npm". On the other hand, the bulk of users are probably fairly computer-literate.

So please pay attention to context cues to understand how to phrase your communication! In the default case, just to give you some idea:

- "evaluation" and "benchmark" are borderline, but OK
- for "JSON" and "assertion" you want to see serious cues from the user that they know what those things are before using them without explaining them

It's OK to briefly explain terms if you're in doubt, and feel free to clarify terms with a short definition if you're unsure if the user will get it.

---

## Creating a skill

### Capture Intent

Start by understanding the user's intent. The current conversation might already contain a workflow the user wants to capture (e.g., they say "turn this into a skill"). If so, extract answers from the conversation history first — the tools used, the sequence of steps, corrections the user made, input/output formats observed. The user may need to fill the gaps, and should confirm before proceeding to the next step.

1. What should this skill enable Claude to do?
2. When should this skill trigger? (what user phrases/contexts)
3. What's the expected output format?
4. Should we set up test cases to verify the skill works? Skills with objectively verifiable outputs (file transforms, data extraction, code generation, fixed workflow steps) benefit from test cases. Skills with subjective outputs (writing style, art) often don't need them. Suggest the appropriate default based on the skill type, but let the user decide.

### Interview and Research

Proactively ask questions about edge cases, input/output formats, example files, success criteria, and dependencies. Wait to write test prompts until you've got this part ironed out.

Check available MCPs - if useful for research (searching docs, finding similar skills, looking up best practices), research in parallel via subagents if available, otherwise inline. Come prepared with context to reduce burden on the user.

### Write the SKILL.md

Based on the user interview, fill in these components:

- **name**: Skill identifier
- **description**: When to trigger, what it does. This is the primary triggering mechanism - include both what the skill does AND specific contexts for when to use it. All "when to use" info goes here, not in the body. Note: currently Claude has a tendency to "undertrigger" skills -- to not use them when they'd be useful. To combat this, please make the skill descriptions a little bit "pushy". So for instance, instead of "How to build a simple fast dashboard to display internal Anthropic data.", you might write "How to build a simple fast dashboard to display internal Anthropic data. Make sure to use this skill whenever the user mentions dashboards, data visualization, internal metrics, or wants to display any kind of company data, even if they don't explicitly ask for a 'dashboard.'"
- **compatibility**: Required tools, dependencies (optional, rarely needed)
- **the rest of the skill :)**

### Skill Writing Guide

#### Anatomy of a Skill

```
skill-name/
├── SKILL.md (required)
│   ├── YAML frontmatter (name, description required)
│   └── Markdown instructions
└── Bundled Resources (optional)
    ├── scripts/    - Executable code for deterministic/repetitive tasks
    ├── references/ - Docs loaded into context as needed
    └── assets/     - Files used in output (templates, icons, fonts)
```

#### Progressive Disclosure

Skills use a three-level loading system:
1. **Metadata** (name + description) - Always in context (~100 words)
2. **SKILL.md body** - In context whenever skill triggers (<500 lines ideal)
3. **Bundled resources** - As needed (unlimited, scripts can execute without loading)

These word counts are approximate and you can feel free to go longer if needed.

**Key patterns:**
- Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines; if you're approaching this limit, add an additional layer of hierarchy along with clear pointers about where the model using the skill should go next to follow up.
- Reference files clearly from SKILL.md with guidance on when to read them
- For large reference files (>300 lines), include a table of contents

**Domain organization**: When a skill supports multiple domains/frameworks, organize by variant:
```
cloud-deploy/
├── SKILL.md (workflow + selection)
└── references/
    ├── aws.md
    ├── gcp.md
    └── azure.md
```
Claude reads only the relevant reference file.

#### Principle of Lack of Surprise

This goes without saying, but skills must not contain malware, exploit code, or any content that could compromise system security. A skill's contents should not surprise the user in their intent if described. Don't go along with requests to create misleading skills or skills designed to facilitate unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or other malicious activities. Things like a "roleplay as an XYZ" are OK though.

#### Writing Patterns

Prefer using the imperative form in instructions.

**Defining output formats** - You can do it like this:
```markdown
## Report structure
ALWAYS use this exact template:
# [Title]
## Executive summary
## Key findings
## Recommendations
```

**Examples pattern** - It's useful to include examples. You can format them like this (but if "Input" and "Output" are in the examples you might want to deviate a little):
```markdown
## Commit message format
**Example 1:**
Input: Added user authentication with JWT tokens
Output: feat(auth): implement JWT-based authentication
```

### Writing Style

Try to explain to the model why things are important in lieu of heavy-handed musty MUSTs. Use theory of mind and try to make the skill general and not super-narrow to specific examples. Start by writing a draft and then look at it with fresh eyes and improve it.

### Test Cases

After writing the skill draft, come up with 2-3 realistic test prompts — the kind of thing a real user would actually say. Share them with the user: [you don't have to use this exact language] "Here are a few test cases I'd like to try. Do these look right, or do you want to add more?" Then run them.

Save test cases to `evals/evals.json`. Don't write assertions yet — just the prompts. You'll draft assertions in the next step while the runs are in progress.

```json
{
  "skill_name": "example-skill",
  "evals": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "prompt": "User's task prompt",
      "expected_output": "Description of expected result",
      "files": []
    }
  ]
}
```

See `references/schemas.md` for the full schema (including the `assertions` field, which you'll add later).

## Running and evaluating test cases

This section is one continuous sequence — don't stop partway through. Do NOT use `/skill-test` or any other testing skill.

Put results in `<skill-name>-workspace/` as a sibling to the skill directory. Within the workspace, organize results by iteration (`iteration-1/`, `iteration-2/`, etc.) and within that, each test case gets a directory (`eval-0/`, `eval-1/`, etc.). Don't create all of this upfront — just create directories as you go.

### Step 1: Spawn all runs (with-skill AND baseline) in the same turn

For each test case, spawn two subagents in the same turn — one with the skill, one without. This is important: don't spawn the with-skill runs first and then come back for baselines later. Launch everything at once so it all finishes around the same time.

**With-skill run:**

```
Execute this task:
- Skill path: <path-to-skill>
- Task: <eval prompt>
- Input files: <eval files if any, or "none">
- Save outputs to: <workspace>/iteration-<N>/eval-<ID>/with_skill/outputs/
- Outputs to save: <what the user cares about — e.g., "the .docx file", "the final CSV">
```

**Baseline run** (same prompt, but the baseline depends on context):
- **Creating a new skill**: no skill at all. Same prompt, no skill path, save to `without_skill/outputs/`.
- **Improving an existing skill**: the old version. Before editing, snapshot the skill (`cp -r <skill-path> <workspace>/skill-snapshot/`), then point the baseline subagent at the snapshot. Save to `old_skill/outputs/`.

Write an `eval_metadata.json` for each test case (assertions can be empty for now). Give each eval a descriptive name based on what it's testing — not just "eval-0". Use this name for the directory too. If this iteration uses new or modified eval prompts, create these files for each new eval directory — don't assume they carry over from previous iterations.

```json
{
  "eval_id": 0,
  "eval_name": "descriptive-name-here",
  "prompt": "The user's task prompt",
  "assertions": []
}
```

### Step 2: While runs are in progress, draft assertions

Don't just wait for the runs to finish — you can use this time productively. Draft quantitative assertions for each test case and explain them to the user. If assertions already exist in `evals/evals.json`, review them and explain what they check.

Good assertions are objectively verifiable and have descriptive names — they should read clearly in the benchmark viewer so someone glancing at the results immediately understands what each one checks. Subjective skills (writing style, design quality) are better evaluated qualitatively — don't force assertions onto things that need human judgment.

Update the `eval_metadata.json` files and `evals/evals.json` with the assertions once drafted. Also explain to the user what they'll see in the viewer — both the qualitative outputs and the quantitative benchmark.

### Step 3: As runs complete, capture timing data

When each subagent task completes, you receive a notification containing `total_tokens` and `duration_ms`. Save this data immediately to `timing.json` in the run directory:

```json
{
  "total_tokens": 84852,
  "duration_ms": 23332,
  "total_duration_seconds": 23.3
}
```

This is the only opportunity to capture this data — it comes through the task notification and isn't persisted elsewhere. Process each notification as it arrives rather than trying to batch them.

### Step 4: Grade, aggregate, and launch the viewer

Once all runs are done:

1. **Grade each run** — spawn a grader subagent (or grade inline) that reads `agents/grader.md` and evaluates each assertion against the outputs. Save results to `grading.json` in each run directory. The grading.json expectations array must use the fields `text`, `passed`, and `evidence` (not `name`/`met`/`details` or other variants) — the viewer depends on these exact field names. For assertions that can be checked programmatically, write and run a script rather than eyeballing it — scripts are faster, more reliable, and can be reused across iterations.

2. **Aggregate into benchmark** — run the aggregation script from the skill-creator directory:
   ```bash
   python -m scripts.aggregate_benchmark <workspace>/iteration-N --skill-name <name>
   ```
   This produces `benchmark.json` and `benchmark.md` with pass_rate, time, and tokens for each configuration, with mean ± stddev and the delta. If generating benchmark.json manually, see `references/schemas.md` for the exact schema the viewer expects.
Put each with_skill version before its baseline counterpart.

3. **Do an analyst pass** — read the benchmark data and surface patterns the aggregate stats might hide. See `agents/analyzer.md` (the "Analyzing Benchmark Results" section) for what to look for — things like assertions that always pass regardless of skill (non-discriminating), high-variance evals (possibly flaky), and time/token tradeoffs.

4. **Launch the viewer** with both qualitative outputs and quantitative data:
   ```bash
   nohup python <skill-creator-path>/eval-viewer/generate_review.py \
     <workspace>/iteration-N \
     --skill-name "my-skill" \
     --benchmark <workspace>/iteration-N/benchmark.json \
     > /dev/null 2>&1 &
   VIEWER_PID=$!
   ```
   For iteration 2+, also pass `--previous-workspace <workspace>/iteration-<N-1>`.

   **Cowork / headless environments:** If `webbrowser.open()` is not available or the environment has no display, use `--static <output_path>` to write a standalone HTML file instead of starting a server. Feedback will be downloaded as a `feedback.json` file when the user clicks "Submit All Reviews". After download, copy `feedback.json` into the workspace directory for the next iteration to pick up.

Note: please use generate_review.py to create the viewer; there's no need to write custom HTML.

5. **Tell the user** something like: "I've opened the results in your browser. There are two tabs — 'Outputs' lets you click through each test case and leave feedback, 'Benchmark' shows the quantitative comparison. When you're done, come back here and let me know."

### What the user sees in the viewer

The "Outputs" tab shows one test case at a time:
- **Prompt**: the task that was given
- **Output**: the files the skill produced, rendered inline where possible
- **Previous Output** (iteration 2+): collapsed section showing last iteration's output
- **Formal Grades** (if grading was run): collapsed section showing assertion pass/fail
- **Feedback**: a textbox that auto-saves as they type
- **Previous Feedback** (iteration 2+): their comments from last time, shown below the textbox

The "Benchmark" tab shows the stats summary: pass rates, timing, and token usage for each configuration, with per-eval breakdowns and analyst observations.

Navigation is via prev/next buttons or arrow keys. When done, they click "Submit All Reviews" which saves all feedback to `feedback.json`.

### Step 5: Read the feedback

When the user tells you they're done, read `feedback.json`:

```json
{
  "reviews": [
    {"run_id": "eval-0-with_skill", "feedback": "the chart is missing axis labels", "timestamp": "..."},
    {"run_id": "eval-1-with_skill", "feedback": "", "timestamp": "..."},
    {"run_id": "eval-2-with_skill", "feedback": "perfect, love this", "timestamp": "..."}
  ],
  "status": "complete"
}
```

Empty feedback means the user thought it was fine. Focus your improvements on the test cases where the user had specific complaints.

Kill the viewer server when you're done with it:

```bash
kill $VIEWER_PID 2>/dev/null
```

---

## Improving the skill

This is the heart of the loop. You've run the test cases, the user has reviewed the results, and now you need to make the skill better based on their feedback.

### How to think about improvements

1. **Generalize from the feedback.** The big picture thing that's happening here is that we're trying to create skills that can be used a million times (maybe literally, maybe even more who knows) across many different prompts. Here you and the user are iterating on only a few examples over and over again because it helps move faster. The user knows these examples in and out and it's quick for them to assess new outputs. But if the skill you and the user are codeveloping works only for those examples, it's useless. Rather than put in fiddly overfitty changes, or oppressively constrictive MUSTs, if there's some stubborn issue, you might try branching out and using different metaphors, or recommending different patterns of working. It's relatively cheap to try and maybe you'll land on something great.

2. **Keep the prompt lean.** Remove things that aren't pulling their weight. Make sure to read the transcripts, not just the final outputs — if it looks like the skill is making the model waste a bunch of time doing things that are unproductive, you can try getting rid of the parts of the skill that are making it do that and seeing what happens.

3. **Explain the why.** Try hard to explain the **why** behind everything you're asking the model to do. Today's LLMs are *smart*. They have good theory of mind and when given a good harness can go beyond rote instructions and really make things happen. Even if the feedback from the user is terse or frustrated, try to actually understand the task and why the user is writing what they wrote, and what they actually wrote, and then transmit this understanding into the instructions. If you find yourself writing ALWAYS or NEVER in all caps, or using super rigid structures, that's a yellow flag — if possible, reframe and explain the reasoning so that the model understands why the thing you're asking for is important. That's a more humane, powerful, and effective approach.

4. **Look for repeated work across test cases.** Read the transcripts from the test runs and notice if the subagents all independently wrote similar helper scripts or took the same multi-step approach to something. If all 3 test cases resulted in the subagent writing a `create_docx.py` or a `build_chart.py`, that's a strong signal the skill should bundle that script. Write it once, put it in `scripts/`, and tell the skill to use it. This saves every future invocation from reinventing the wheel.

This task is pretty important (we are trying to create billions a year in economic value here!) and your thinking time is not the blocker; take your time and really mull things over. I'd suggest writing a draft revision and then looking at it anew and making improvements. Really do your best to get into the head of the user and understand what they want and need.

### The iteration loop

After improving the skill:

1. Apply your improvements to the skill
2. Rerun all test cases into a new `iteration-<N+1>/` directory, including baseline runs. If you're creating a new skill, the baseline is always `without_skill` (no skill) — that stays the same across iterations. If you're improving an existing skill, use your judgment on what makes sense as the baseline: the original version the user came in with, or the previous iteration.
3. Launch the reviewer with `--previous-workspace` pointing at the previous iteration
4. Wait for the user to review and tell you they're done
5. Read the new feedback, improve again, repeat

Keep going until:
- The user says they're happy
- The feedback is all empty (everything looks good)
- You're not making meaningful progress

---

## Advanced: Blind comparison

For situations where you want a more rigorous comparison between two versions of a skill (e.g., the user asks "is the new version actually better?"), there's a blind comparison system. Read `agents/comparator.md` and `agents/analyzer.md` for the details. The basic idea is: give two outputs to an independent agent without telling it which is which, and let it judge quality. Then analyze why the winner won.

This is optional, requires subagents, and most users won't need it. The human review loop is usually sufficient.

---

## Description Optimization

The description field in SKILL.md frontmatter is the primary mechanism that determines whether Claude invokes a skill. After creating or improving a skill, offer to optimize the description for better triggering accuracy.

### Step 1: Generate trigger eval queries

Create 20 eval queries — a mix of should-trigger and should-not-trigger. Save as JSON:

```json
[
  {"query": "the user prompt", "should_trigger": true},
  {"query": "another prompt", "should_trigger": false}
]
```

The queries must be realistic and something a Claude Code or Claude.ai user would actually type. Not abstract requests, but requests that are concrete and specific and have a good amount of detail. For instance, file paths, personal context about the user's job or situation, column names and values, company names, URLs. A little bit of backstory. Some might be in lowercase or contain abbreviations or typos or casual speech. Use a mix of different lengths, and focus on edge cases rather than making them clear-cut (the user will get a chance to sign off on them).

Bad: `"Format this data"`, `"Extract text from PDF"`, `"Create a chart"`

Good: `"ok so my boss just sent me this xlsx file (its in my downloads, called something like 'Q4 sales final FINAL v2.xlsx') and she wants me to add a column that shows the profit margin as a percentage. The revenue is in column C and costs are in column D i think"`

For the **should-trigger** queries (8-10), think about coverage. You want different phrasings of the same intent — some formal, some casual. Include cases where the user doesn't explicitly name the skill or file type but clearly needs it. Throw in some uncommon use cases and cases where this skill competes with another but should win.

For the **should-not-trigger** queries (8-10), the most valuable ones are the near-misses — queries that share keywords or concepts with the skill but actually need something different. Think adjacent domains, ambiguous phrasing where a naive keyword match would trigger but shouldn't, and cases where the query touches on something the skill does but in a context where another tool is more appropriate.

The key thing to avoid: don't make should-not-trigger queries obviously irrelevant. "Write a fibonacci function" as a negative test for a PDF skill is too easy — it doesn't test anything. The negative cases should be genuinely tricky.

### Step 2: Review with user

Present the eval set to the user for review using the HTML template:

1. Read the template from `assets/eval_review.html`
2. Replace the placeholders:
   - `__EVAL_DATA_PLACEHOLDER__` → the JSON array of eval items (no quotes around it — it's a JS variable assignment)
   - `__SKILL_NAME_PLACEHOLDER__` → the skill's name
   - `__SKILL_DESCRIPTION_PLACEHOLDER__` → the skill's current description
3. Write to a temp file (e.g., `/tmp/eval_review_<skill-name>.html`) and open it: `open /tmp/eval_review_<skill-name>.html`
4. The user can edit queries, toggle should-trigger, add/remove entries, then click "Export Eval Set"
5. The file downloads to `~/Downloads/eval_set.json` — check the Downloads folder for the most recent version in case there are multiple (e.g., `eval_set (1).json`)

This step matters — bad eval queries lead to bad descriptions.

### Step 3: Run the optimization loop

Tell the user: "This will take some time — I'll run the optimization loop in the background and check on it periodically."

Save the eval set to the workspace, then run in the background:

```bash
python -m scripts.run_loop \
  --eval-set <path-to-trigger-eval.json> \
  --skill-path <path-to-skill> \
  --model <model-id-powering-this-session> \
  --max-iterations 5 \
  --verbose
```

Use the model ID from your system prompt (the one powering the current session) so the triggering test matches what the user actually experiences.

While it runs, periodically tail the output to give the user updates on which iteration it's on and what the scores look like.

This handles the full optimization loop automatically. It splits the eval set into 60% train and 40% held-out test, evaluates the current description (running each query 3 times to get a reliable trigger rate), then calls Claude to propose improvements based on what failed. It re-evaluates each new description on both train and test, iterating up to 5 times. When it's done, it opens an HTML report in the browser showing the results per iteration and returns JSON with `best_description` — selected by test score rather than train score to avoid overfitting.

### How skill triggering works

Understanding the triggering mechanism helps design better eval queries. Skills appear in Claude's `available_skills` list with their name + description, and Claude decides whether to consult a skill based on that description. The important thing to know is that Claude only consults skills for tasks it can't easily handle on its own — simple, one-step queries like "read this PDF" may not trigger a skill even if the description matches perfectly, because Claude can handle them directly with basic tools. Complex, multi-step, or specialized queries reliably trigger skills when the description matches.

This means your eval queries should be substantive enough that Claude would actually benefit from consulting a skill. Simple queries like "read file X" are poor test cases — they won't trigger skills regardless of description quality.

### Step 4: Apply the result

Take `best_description` from the JSON output and update the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter. Show the user before/after and report the scores.

---

### Package and Present (only if `present_files` tool is available)

Check whether you have access to the `present_files` tool. If you don't, skip this step. If you do, package the skill and present the .skill file to the user:

```bash
python -m scripts.package_skill <path/to/skill-folder>
```

After packaging, direct the user to the resulting `.skill` file path so they can install it.

---

## Claude.ai-specific instructions

In Claude.ai, the core workflow is the same (draft → test → review → improve → repeat), but because Claude.ai doesn't have subagents, some mechanics change. Here's what to adapt:

**Running test cases**: No subagents means no parallel execution. For each test case, read the skill's SKILL.md, then follow its instructions to accomplish the test prompt yourself. Do them one at a time. This is less rigorous than independent subagents (you wrote the skill and you're also running it, so you have full context), but it's a useful sanity check — and the human review step compensates. Skip the baseline runs — just use the skill to complete the task as requested.

**Reviewing results**: If you can't open a browser (e.g., Claude.ai's VM has no display, or you're on a remote server), skip the browser reviewer entirely. Instead, present results directly in the conversation. For each test case, show the prompt and the output. If the output is a file the user needs to see (like a .docx or .xlsx), save it to the filesystem and tell them where it is so they can download and inspect it. Ask for feedback inline: "How does this look? Anything you'd change?"

**Benchmarking**: Skip the quantitative benchmarking — it relies on baseline comparisons which aren't meaningful without subagents. Focus on qualitative feedback from the user.

**The iteration loop**: Same as before — improve the skill, rerun the test cases, ask for feedback — just without the browser reviewer in the middle. You can still organize results into iteration directories on the filesystem if you have one.

**Description optimization**: This section requires the `claude` CLI tool (specifically `claude -p`) which is only available in Claude Code. Skip it if you're on Claude.ai.

**Blind comparison**: Requires subagents. Skip it.

**Packaging**: The `package_skill.py` script works anywhere with Python and a filesystem. On Claude.ai, you can run it and the user can download the resulting `.skill` file.

**Updating an existing skill**: The user might be asking you to update an existing skill, not create a new one. In this case:
- **Preserve the original name.** Note the skill's directory name and `name` frontmatter field -- use them unchanged. E.g., if the installed skill is `research-helper`, output `research-helper.skill` (not `research-helper-v2`).
- **Copy to a writeable location before editing.** The installed skill path may be read-only. Copy to `/tmp/skill-name/`, edit there, and package from the copy.
- **If packaging manually, stage in `/tmp/` first**, then copy to the output directory -- direct writes may fail due to permissions.

---

## Cowork-Specific Instructions

If you're in Cowork, the main things to know are:

- You have subagents, so the main workflow (spawn test cases in parallel, run baselines, grade, etc.) all works. (However, if you run into severe problems with timeouts, it's OK to run the test prompts in series rather than parallel.)
- You don't have a browser or display, so when generating the eval viewer, use `--static <output_path>` to write a standalone HTML file instead of starting a server. Then proffer a link that the user can click to open the HTML in their browser.
- For whatever reason, the Cowork setup seems to disincline Claude from generating the eval viewer after running the tests, so just to reiterate: whether you're in Cowork or in Claude Code, after running tests, you should always generate the eval viewer for the human to look at examples before revising the skill yourself and trying to make corrections, using `generate_review.py` (not writing your own boutique html code). Sorry in advance but I'm gonna go all caps here: GENERATE THE EVAL VIEWER *BEFORE* evaluating inputs yourself. You want to get them in front of the human ASAP!
- Feedback works differently: since there's no running server, the viewer's "Submit All Reviews" button will download `feedback.json` as a file. You can then read it from there (you may have to request access first).
- Packaging works — `package_skill.py` just needs Python and a filesystem.
- Description optimization (`run_loop.py` / `run_eval.py`) should work in Cowork just fine since it uses `claude -p` via subprocess, not a browser, but please save it until you've fully finished making the skill and the user agrees it's in good shape.
- **Updating an existing skill**: The user might be asking you to update an existing skill, not create a new one. Follow the update guidance in the claude.ai section above.

---

## Reference files

The agents/ directory contains instructions for specialized subagents. Read them when you need to spawn the relevant subagent.

- `agents/grader.md` — How to evaluate assertions against outputs
- `agents/comparator.md` — How to do blind A/B comparison between two outputs
- `agents/analyzer.md` — How to analyze why one version beat another

The references/ directory has additional documentation:
- `references/schemas.md` — JSON structures for evals.json, grading.json, etc.

---

Repeating one more time the core loop here for emphasis:

- Figure out what the skill is about
- Draft or edit the skill
- Run claude-with-access-to-the-skill on test prompts
- With the user, evaluate the outputs:
  - Create benchmark.json and run `eval-viewer/generate_review.py` to help the user review them
  - Run quantitative evals
- Repeat until you and the user are satisfied
- Package the final skill and return it to the user.

```text
112	func navigationDirectory(path string) (string, error) {
113		info, err := os.Stat(path)
114		if err != nil {
115			return "", fmt.Errorf("inspect navigation directory %q: %w", path, err)
116		}
117		if !info.IsDir() {
118			return "", fmt.Errorf("navigation target %q is not a directory", path)
119		}
120		canonical, err := pathx.Canonical(path)
121		if err != nil {
122			return "", fmt.Errorf("canonicalize navigation directory %q: %w", path, err)
123		}
124		return canonical, nil
125	}
126	
127	// navigationIdentity compares known paths, including native case/path aliases.
128	// SameFile compares current paths, not an earlier directory identity snapshot.
129	func navigationIdentity(label, actual, expected string) error {
130		if expected == "" {
131			return nil
132		}
133		canonical, err := pathx.Canonical(expected)
134		if err != nil {
135			return fmt.Errorf("canonicalize expected %s: %w", label, err)
136		}
137		if actual == canonical {
138			return nil
139		}
140		actualInfo, actualErr := os.Stat(actual)
141		expectedInfo, expectedErr := os.Stat(canonical)
142		if actualErr == nil && expectedErr == nil && os.SameFile(actualInfo, expectedInfo) {
143			return nil
144		}
145		return fmt.Errorf("%s changed: expected %q, found %q", label, canonical, actual)
146	}

148	func discoverNavigationRepository(ctx context.Context, path, bareCommonDir string) (gitx.Repo, error) {
149		repository, err := gitx.Discover(ctx, path)
150		if ctx.Err() != nil {
151			return gitx.Repo{}, ctx.Err()
152		}
153		if err != nil && isBareDir(path) {
154			// Discover requests --show-toplevel, which Git rejects for a bare hub.
155			// Verify its identity with Git rather than accepting the skeleton alone.
156			out, probeErr := gitx.RunReadOnly(ctx, path, "rev-parse", "--path-format=absolute", "--git-dir", "--git-common-dir", "--is-bare-repository")
157			if ctx.Err() != nil {
158				return gitx.Repo{}, ctx.Err()
159			}
160			if probeErr != nil {
161				return gitx.Repo{}, probeErr
162			}
163			fields := strings.Split(out, "\n")
164			if len(fields) != 3 || fields[2] != "true" {
165				return gitx.Repo{}, fmt.Errorf("cannot verify bare repository %q", path)
166			}
167			gitDir, canonicalErr := pathx.Canonical(fields[0])
168			if canonicalErr != nil {
169				return gitx.Repo{}, canonicalErr
170			}
171			commonDir, canonicalErr := pathx.Canonical(fields[1])
172			if canonicalErr != nil {
173				return gitx.Repo{}, canonicalErr
174			}
175			repository = gitx.Repo{GitDir: gitDir, GitCommonDir: commonDir, MainRoot: commonDir, Bare: true}
176			err = nil
177		} else if err != nil && bareCommonDir != "" {
178			// Discover assumes a linked checkout's main root is a working tree.
179			// Here the caller has freshly verified both the bare hub and this
180			// checkout's registration, so probe the checkout's exact Git identity
181			// without asking Discover to find a non-bare main checkout.
182			out, probeErr := gitx.RunReadOnly(ctx, path, "rev-parse", "--path-format=absolute", "--show-toplevel", "--git-dir", "--git-common-dir")
183			if ctx.Err() != nil {
184				return gitx.Repo{}, ctx.Err()
185			}
186			if probeErr != nil {
187				return gitx.Repo{}, probeErr
188			}
189			fields := strings.Split(out, "\n")
190			if len(fields) != 3 {
191				return gitx.Repo{}, fmt.Errorf("cannot verify checkout %q of bare repository", path)
192			}
193			for i := range fields {
194				fields[i], probeErr = pathx.Canonical(fields[i])
195				if probeErr != nil {
196					return gitx.Repo{}, probeErr
197				}
198			}
199			if err := navigationIdentity("checkout Git common directory", fields[2], bareCommonDir); err != nil {
200				return gitx.Repo{}, err
201			}
202			repository = gitx.Repo{Root: fields[0], GitDir: fields[1], GitCommonDir: fields[2], MainRoot: bareCommonDir, IsLinkedWorktree: fields[1] != fields[2]}
203			err = nil
204		}
205		if err != nil {
206			return gitx.Repo{}, err
207		}
208		root := repository.Root
209		if repository.Bare {
210			root = repository.GitCommonDir
211		}
212		// Discover also succeeds inside a checkout; navigation must validate the
213		// selected directory itself, not silently accept an enclosing repository.
214		if err := navigationIdentity("Git root", root, path); err != nil {
215			return gitx.Repo{}, err
216		}
217		return repository, nil
218	}
```

8	
9	# TUI, repositories, quick notes, and bootstrap
10	
11	Bare `dev` opens an interactive dashboard when standard input/output are terminals. When piped, it prints the plain task listing so shell composition remains predictable.
12	
13	There are three independent full-screen models. Bare `dev` / `dev tui` is the
14	eight-view inventory dashboard below. Preview-labelled `dev repo flow [repo]` is a
15	TTY-only, plan-first lifecycle view for one canonical repository; it is not a
16	dashboard tab or mode. `dev triage` is the cross-repository organizer.
17	
18	## Eight views
19	
20	REPOS and REMOTE support `y u` (also row action **copy clone URL**). REPOS reads
21	the selected checkout's fetch URLs locally, preferring origin and asking when
22	multiple choices remain. REMOTE copies CloneURL, falling back only to SSHURL,
23	not the browser URL. Missing/unsafe URLs, stale selections and clipboard errors
24	do not trigger clone/fetch or an empty copy. To add the selected repository as a
25	dependency, use the CLI [submodule addition wizard](submodule-workspaces.md#add-a-repository-as-a-submodule);
26	the dashboard does not add submodules itself.
27	
28	| View | Question | Source |
29	|---|---|---|
30	| TASKS | What am I working on? | task registry plus live Git/runtime facts |
31	| REPOS | What durable repositories exist here? | configured scan roots and local catalog |
32	| FLEET | What exists and is active on configured machines? | accepted local REPOS snapshot plus remote `dev` snapshots over SSH |
33	| TRY | Which experiments can I resume, archive, or graduate? | experiment catalog plus live facts |
34	| REMOTE | What can I open or clone? | authenticated `gh`/`glab` inventories and cache |
35	| SKILLS | Which skills would an agent launched from this context read? | context-first targets plus an `A` all-repositories toggle |
36	| MCP | Which MCP declarations would that context expose? | sanitized static configuration with the same shared scope |
37	| SSH | How do I connect to a machine? | local aliases, canonical registry, cached discovery and provider membership |
38	
39	The initial TASKS frame is built before runtime auto-detection, project-root
40	lookup, cache decoding, shell tool probes, or the optional release refresh can
41	finish. TASKS, REPOS, and TRY then publish independently from one shared local
42	cycle. REMOTE, SKILLS, MCP, and SSH stay lazy; FLEET uses delayed host-by-host warming. Each requested view has a generation:
43	`r` supersedes the previous read, late results are ignored, failed refreshes keep
44	usable rows visible, and a successful empty result removes obsolete rows. Cache
45	acceptance and current live completion are distinct; there is no all-tabs-ready
46	state for optional views that may never be opened.
47	
48	Use an absolute path that does not exist for a one-run diagnostic trace:
49	
50	```bash
51	DEV_TUI_TRACE=/tmp/dev-tui-trace.json dev
52	```
53	
54	The private, bounded JSON is written after the alternate screen is restored. It
55	contains relative timings, aggregate row counts, and categorical
56	view/generation/outcome fields, never repository/task/host/tool names, paths,
57	commands, key values, URLs, handles, or
58	raw errors. It is not `stats.db` and is never sent anywhere.
59	`tui.initial_view_returned` means the Bubble Tea view string was built, not that
60	the terminal rasterized it.
61	
62	Switch with `tab`, `h`/`l`, arrows, or left-click a visible tab. A left-button
63	press selects a visible row; clicking the selected row opens its actions, even
64	when selection came from the keyboard or startup. No double-click timing is needed.
65	The wheel moves three rows, and a right-button press selects a row then opens its
66	actions. Modified row clicks, motion and releases do not activate rows. Opening the menu does
67	not execute an option. Enter/`o` opens the row. Some terminals require Shift/Option for native
68	text selection while mouse tracking is enabled.
69	
70	## Live list filtering
71	
72	In all eight dashboard views, `/` narrows the list as you type. Up/Down selects
73	visible results while the input remains focused, without changing the query or
74	its text cursor, running an action, or initiating a network request. `j/k` and
75	other letters remain search text. Left/Right/Home/End move the text cursor;
76	cursor-only edits and deletions that change nothing retain the selected result.
77	Only an actual query change selects the first result.
78	
79	Enter keeps the query and selection and exits input; it does not open the row.
80	Press Enter again from the list to use the selected row's normal open action.
81	Esc while filtering clears the query. The input and its key hints remain visible
82	even when the selected repository has pending observations. Notes search still
83	waits for Enter before querying; forms, SSH dialogs and Ctrl+O action search keep
84	their separate behavior.
85	
86	## Contextual Help (v0.2.24)
87	
88	Press `?` or click **Help** in the footer. Help starts on **Keys** for the current
89	dashboard view, keeping that view's TL;DR at the top. It has three tabs:
90	
91	| Tab | Content |
92	|---|---|
93	| Keys | This view's actions, common navigation and configured tools, including availability and conditions |
94	| Guide | Workflow, columns, colors and symbols; a read-only selected-row snapshot captured when Help opened |
95	| Manual | All embedded `dev help` topics, with related topics first, plus the shared workflow TL;DR |
96	
97	Keys and Guide share a search over their entries, with shortcut matches before
98	guide matches. Search is limited to the selected help view; choose **All views**
99	to search all eight. Changing help scope does not change the actual dashboard
100	tab, selection, filter or order. The selected-row explanation appears only for
101	the view where Help opened and retains unknown, loading or cached observations.
102	It is an explanation of that captured display, never fresh action authority.
103	
104	In REPOS, Guide explains why cyan/blue selection overrides the row's usual
105	color, orange reports dirty paths, and gray alone does not prove Git clean.
106	It covers `⇡N`/`⇣N`/`⇕`, `=N`, `+N`, `!N`, `?N`, `clean`/`local`, unknown `?`,
107	cached `~`, loading/truncated `…`, and each column's `—`. LIVE, WT, task counts,
108	logical owned SIZE and LATEST all have separate explanations. Other views have
109	their own legends: for example, green MCP means enabled configuration, not a
110	running or healthy server. Color appearance follows the terminal palette and
111	`--color` settings.
112	
113	Manual search covers topic names, titles, headings and body text, with excerpts.
114	Open a result to read it at the matching passage. Paragraphs wrap; code, ASCII
115	diagrams and tables preserve their structure and can pan horizontally. `/`
116	finds text within an article and `n`/`N` moves between matches. Back preserves the
117	previous query and reading position. Each article names its CLI counterpart.
118	
119	Use `1–3` or click tabs, `v` or click **View** for scope, `/` or click the search
120	field, `j/k` to choose or scroll, and Enter to read an entry. PgUp/PgDn, the wheel
121	and the clickable/draggable scrollbar move through long content. Article pan
122	controls and left/right arrows reveal wide code or diagrams. Esc stops search
123	editing, then clears the query, returns a level and finally closes Help. `q`
124	closes outside text input; letters such as `q`, `v` and `f` stay text while typing.
125	In a live Help index/results search, Up/Down selects entries without leaving the
126	input or moving its text cursor, and `j/k` remain text. Cursor-only edits keep the
127	selected result; only changed text resets it. Enter keeps the query and selection
128	without opening an entry; press Enter again outside input to read it. Article
129	find/scroll keeps its existing Enter-submit and `n`/`N` match navigation.
130	
131	Help and Ctrl+O share a floating popup with **Expand** and **Close**. Its normal
132	maximum is 104 columns × 32 rows, leaving at least two cells around it; below
133	80 columns or 22 rows it fills the screen. `f` expands Help. Click outside to
134	close without activating a background row. Popup scrollbar dragging is supported
135	even though dashboard row activation ignores mouse motion.
136	
137	Opening and searching Help uses only embedded documents, existing tool
138	availability and the captured dashboard state. It starts no Git, forge, runtime,
139	provider or MCP probes. Flow and triage retain their independent help interfaces.
140	
141	## Startup repository and discovery (v0.2.24)
142	
143	TASKS remains the startup view. The first REPOS visit selects the repository
144	containing the startup directory without changing ordering, scrolling it into
145	view when needed. Subdirectories, aliases and linked worktrees resolve through
146	Git common-directory identity; linked worktrees select the repo parent row.
147	Manual selection, filtering and sorting take precedence over delayed results.
148	
149	An outside startup Git repo gets clickable **Add this repo…** and **Scan parent
150	directory…** entries, also in Ctrl+O. The first appends the main repo root to
151	`paths.repo_paths`; the second appends that root's parent to `paths.scan_roots`
152	and includes sibling projects under the normal depth-3 discovery rules. Neither
153	uses a nested working directory as the candidate root. Prefer exact repo entries
154	for isolated locations and scan roots for directories dedicated to projects.
155	
156	Both actions preview the actual configuration file (including `--config`), path,
157	scope and field change, with clickable confirm/cancel. Scroll long preview details
158	with the wheel over the text or PgUp/PgDn. Only the selected field is extended;
159	existing comments, entry order and inherited defaults are retained. Already covered
160	repos are not added again, and old entries are not automatically consolidated.
161	Saving reloads local discovery and selects the added repo. Failed/incomplete scans
162	remain unknown rather than becoming an enrollment suggestion.
163	
164	Automatic writes use the guarded macOS/Linux file backend, retaining metadata and
165	private recovery in `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dev/config-recovery`. A concurrent edit or
166	changed repository identity rejects the preview. Symlink configurations, unsupported
167	TOML layouts or platforms offer a manual change and config editor instead.
168	If saving succeeds but reload fails, the dashboard reports both outcomes.
169	
170	## Common actions
171	
172	### TASKS
173	
174	```text
175	enter/o   open the selected task
176	p         park warm and enter the next action
177	c         edit the next action
178	n/N       quick-add / browse repository notes
179	ctrl+o    task state filters
180	```
````

10	# TUI、Repository、Quick Notes 與 Bootstrap
11

15	Standard input/output 都是 terminal 時，直接執行 `dev` 會開啟 interactive dashboard；透過 pipe 執行時會輸出 plain task listing，讓 shell composition 保持可預期。
16	
17	`dev repo flow [repo]` 是另一個獨立、僅限 TTY 且標示為 preview 的全螢幕介面，不是 dashboard 的 tab 或 view。它聚焦單一 canonical repository 的所有 registered worktrees 與 task-only rows，並把 lifecycle intent、live evidence 與 plan-first actions 並列；完整說明見 [Repository Flow 預覽](repository-flow.zh-TW.md)。
18	
19	## 八個 view
20	
21	REPOS／REMOTE 支援 `y u`，row action menu 也有 **copy clone URL**。REPOS 只在
22	本機讀取選中 checkout 的 fetch URL，優先 origin，多個候選時要求選擇。REMOTE
23	複製 CloneURL，其次 SSHURL，不拿瀏覽器 URL 代替。缺少／不安全的 URL、stale
24	selection 與 clipboard 錯誤不會觸發 clone／fetch 或複製空字串。要加入 dependency，
25	請用 CLI 的 [submodule 新增 wizard](submodule-workspaces.zh-TW.md)；dashboard
26	本身不新增 submodule。
27	
28	| View | 回答問題 | 來源 |
29	|---|---|---|
30	| TASKS | 我正在處理什麼？ | task registry 加即時 Git/runtime facts |
31	| REPOS | 本機有哪些持久 repositories？ | 設定的 scan roots 與 local catalog |
32	| FLEET | 設定的機器上有哪些 repository 與 active work？ | 已接受的 local REPOS snapshot 加上透過 SSH 取得的 remote `dev` snapshots |
33	| TRY | 哪些 experiments 能 resume、archive 或 graduate？ | experiment catalog 加 live facts |
34	| REMOTE | 有哪些 repository 能 open 或 clone？ | authenticated `gh`/`glab` inventories 與 cache |
35	| SKILLS | 從目前 context 啟動 agent 時會讀到哪些 skills？ | context-first targets 加 `A` all-repositories toggle |
36	| MCP | 該 context 會暴露哪些 MCP declarations？ | 使用相同 shared scope 的 sanitized static config |
37	| SSH | 如何連到某台機器？ | local aliases、canonical registry、cached discovery 與 provider membership |
38	
39	初始 TASKS frame 會先建立，不等待 runtime auto-detection、project-root lookup、
40	cache decode、shell tool probe 或 optional release refresh 完成。TASKS、REPOS 與
41	TRY 接著由同一個 shared local cycle 獨立發布；REMOTE、SKILLS、MCP 與 SSH 維持
42	lazy，FLEET 則延後逐台預熱。每個被請求的 view 都有自己的 generation：`r` 會 supersede 舊讀取，晚到
43	結果會被忽略，refresh 失敗時保留可用 rows，而成功的空結果會移除過時 rows。
44	Cache acceptance 與目前 live load completion 是不同階段；可能從未開啟的 optional
45	view 不存在虛構的 all-tabs-ready 狀態。
46	
47	單次診斷 trace 必須指定一個尚不存在的 absolute path：
48	
49	```bash
50	DEV_TUI_TRACE=/tmp/dev-tui-trace.json dev
51	```
52	
53	Private、bounded JSON 會在 alternate screen 還原後才寫入。內容只有 relative timing、
54	aggregate row counts 與 categorical view/generation/outcome fields，不包含 repository/task/host/tool
55	名稱、paths、commands、key values、URLs、handles 或 raw errors。它不是
56	`stats.db`，也不會送出本機。`tui.initial_view_returned` 只代表 Bubble Tea view
57	string 已建立，不代表 terminal 已 rasterize。
58	
59	用 `tab`、`h`/`l`、左右鍵，或 left-click visible tab 切換。Left-button
60	press 選取 visible row；點目前反白列就開啟 actions，包含鍵盤或啟動時預選的列，
61	不限兩次點擊間隔。Wheel 每次移動三列；right-button press 先選取 row，再開啟
62	該 row 的 actions。Modified row click、motion 與 release 不會啟動列；開啟選單的點擊
63	只開選單，另行點選項目才執行。Enter/`o` 開啟目標。Mouse tracking
64	啟用時，部分 terminal 的原生文字選取需要按住 Shift/Option。
65	
66	## 即時篩選清單
67	
68	八個 dashboard views 都可按 `/` 邊輸入邊篩選。輸入時用上下鍵選取可見結果，
69	輸入框仍保持焦點，查詢文字與文字游標不變，也不執行操作或觸發網路請求。
70	`j/k` 與其他字母仍是搜尋文字。左右鍵、Home/End 只移動文字游標；只移動游標
71	或未刪除任何字元時，保留目前結果選取。只有查詢文字真的改變才選取第一筆。
72	
73	Enter 保留查詢與選取並離開輸入，不會開啟該列；回到清單後再按 Enter，才執行
74	所選列原本的開啟操作。篩選時按 Esc 會清除查詢。即使所選 repository 尚有
75	pending observations，輸入框與按鍵提示仍會顯示。Notes 搜尋仍需 Enter 才送出
76	查詢；forms、SSH dialogs 與 Ctrl+O action search 保留各自的行為。
77	
78	## 目前分頁的 Help（v0.2.24）
79	
80	按 `?` 或點 footer 的 **Help**，預設開啟目前 dashboard 分頁的 **Keys**，
81	頂部保留該頁的 TL;DR。Help 分成三個頁籤：
82	
83	| 頁籤 | 內容 |
84	|---|---|
85	| Keys | 本頁操作、通用導覽與已設定的工具，包含可用狀態及必要條件 |
86	| Guide | 使用流程、欄位、顏色與符號；開啟 Help 時擷取的所選列唯讀快照 |
87	| Manual | 全部內嵌 `dev help` 主題，相關主題優先，另有共用 workflow TL;DR |
88	
89	Keys 與 Guide 共用搜尋，先列快捷鍵、再列說明。預設只搜尋選定的 Help
90	分頁；選 **All views** 才搜尋七頁。切換說明範圍不改變實際 dashboard
91	分頁、選取、filter 或排序。所選列的解讀只出現在開啟 Help 時的那一頁，
92	保留 unknown、loading 與 cached 狀態；它說明擷取時的畫面，不能當成
93	執行操作的新證據。
94	
95	REPOS 的 Guide 解釋：青／藍色選取會覆蓋原列色，橘色表示 dirty paths，
96	不能只憑灰色判定 Git clean。另包含 `⇡N`／`⇣N`／`⇕`、`=N`、`+N`、`!N`、
97	`?N`、`clean`／`local`、未知 `?`、舊快照 `~`、載入或截短 `…`，以及各欄
98	`—` 的不同含義。LIVE、WT、task 數量、logical owned SIZE 與 LATEST
99	各有說明。其他分頁有自己的圖例，例如 MCP 綠色表示設定啟用，不能推斷

102	Manual 搜尋主題名稱、標題、小節與全文，並顯示摘錄；開啟結果會定位到
103	命中段落。一般段落換行，程式碼、ASCII 圖與表格保留結構並支援橫向捲動。
104	文章內 `/` 查找、`n`／`N` 切換命中；Back 保留上一層搜尋與閱讀位置。
105	每篇文章都標示對應的 CLI 指令。
106	
107	用 `1–3` 或點頁籤切換，`v` 或點 **View** 選範圍，`/` 或點搜尋欄輸入，

109	瀏覽長內容；文章的橫向捲動按鈕或左右鍵可查看過寬的程式碼與圖。

112	在即時 Help 索引／結果搜尋中，上下鍵選取項目，不離開輸入或移動文字游標；
113	`j/k` 仍是文字。只移動文字游標會保留選取，只有文字改變才重設結果。Enter
114	保留查詢與選取，不會開啟項目；離開輸入後再按 Enter 才閱讀。文章內查找／捲動

120	dashboard 列啟動仍忽略 mouse motion。
121	
122	開啟與搜尋 Help 只讀內嵌文章、既有工具可用狀態及畫面快照，不另行探測
123	Git、forge、runtime、provider 或 MCP。Flow 與 triage 維持各自的 Help。
124	
125	## 啟動 repo 與掃描設定（v0.2.24）
126	
127	啟動時仍顯示 TASKS。首次切到 REPOS 時，預選啟動目錄所屬的 repository，
128	保留原排序並讓該列出現在可視範圍。子目錄、alias 與 linked worktree 透過
129	Git common directory 對應；linked worktree 選取 repo 主列。使用者手動選取、
130	篩選或排序後，晚到的資料不會再把游標拉回啟動 repo。
131	
132	啟動所在 Git repo 未被掃描設定涵蓋時，REPOS 顯示可點擊的 **Add this repo…**
133	與 **Scan parent directory…**，Ctrl+O 也提供相同入口。前者把主 repo 根目錄加入
134	`paths.repo_paths`，後者把該根目錄的父目錄加入 `paths.scan_roots`，依原有最大
135	深度 3 的規則掃描同層專案，不使用目前子目錄當候選根目錄。零散位置優先用
136	repo_paths；專門集中存放專案的目錄適合用 scan_roots。
137	
138	兩種操作都先預覽實際設定檔（尊重 `--config`）、路徑、範圍與欄位變更，並提供
139	可點擊的確認／取消。較長的預覽可在文字上使用滾輪或 PgUp/PgDn 捲動。
140	只追加所選欄位，保留註解、項目順序與省略欄位繼承的預設值；避免重複加入，
141	不自動合併或刪除既有項目。儲存後重新載入本機清單並選取新加入的 repo。
142	掃描失敗或不完整維持未知，不會直接當成未納管提示加入。
143	
144	自動寫入使用 macOS/Linux 的 guarded file backend，保留 metadata，並在
145	`$XDG_DATA_HOME/dev/config-recovery` 保存私有復原紀錄。設定檔被同時編輯或
146	repo 身分改變時拒絕套用舊預覽。Symlink 設定檔、不支援的 TOML 格式或平台
147	會提供手動修改內容與設定編輯器入口。若儲存成功但重載失敗，會分別回報。
148	
149	## 常用 actions
150	
151	### TASKS
152	
153	```text
154	enter/o   開啟選取的 task
155	p         park warm 並輸入 next action
156	c         編輯 next action
157	n/N       quick-add／瀏覽 repository notes
158	ctrl+o    task state filters
159	```
160	
161	COLD worktree task 必須透過 `dev work resume` 重建；TUI 不會用 generic open action 靜默重建。若 worktree 已遺失或不再由 Git 註冊，必須先執行 `dev work sweep`，讓它在 resume 或 reap 前回報需要 salvage 的 agent artifacts。Enter 不會開啟只剩 artifacts 的 abandoned directory。Terminal 寬度至少 97 cells 時，TASKS table 會顯示 display-width-aware `REPO` column；更窄時保留原 columns，並在 detail 顯示 repo/path。
162	
163	### REPOS
164	
165	```text
166	enter/o   ad-hoc open，不建立 task
167	n         透過 clone-aware `repo new` wizard 建立 repository
168	a/N       quick-add／瀏覽 repository notes
169	space     展開 linked worktrees
170	m         編輯 repository tags/summary
171	d         追蹤目前 branch 的 direct work
172	s         啟動 isolated work：branch + worktree + provisioning + runtime
173	H         開啟 repository activity heatmap
174	y         開啟 copy/context actions
175	```
176	
177	展開後會顯示每個 linked worktree，包括 harness-owned `(ephemeral)` 與未受管理的 `(external)` checkout。LIVE column 將 runtime activity 與 task state 分開。
178	
179	REPOS 為空、篩選後無結果，或所選列尚有 pending observations 時，仍可按 `n`
180	或 Ctrl+O → new repository。這個入口不依賴所選列，選單開啟期間該列消失也不會
````

```text
18	### Added
19	
20	- `dev repo cd <repo>` provides shell-only repository navigation, equivalent

25	  independent Try clone. Large repositories default to authored/requested-review
26	  requests; navigation never preloads PR lists or details.

28	  dashboard services. Squash merge binds the reviewed head and retains unknown
29	  outcomes without retries; optional base sync uses guarded fast-forward or
30	  explicitly chosen rebase, with separate partial results and no local cleanup.

32	  including uncloned REMOTE rows, while retaining native gh-dash configuration.
```

1020	
1021	Bare `dev` (or `dev tui`) opens eight lists, switched with `tab`:
1022	
1023	- **TASKS** — the change streams dev is tracking. What am I working on.
1024	- **REPOS** — durable repositories under the scan roots, with branch, dirty
1025	  state, owned size, runtime, worktrees and task tally. What do I have here.
1026	- **FLEET** — an expandable remote host tree with cached repositories and a
1027	  separate HERDR registration/enabled column. Local is hidden by default; `a`
1028	  reveals it at the end. Host actions provide SSH, dotfile status, and exact
1029	  Herdr profile enable/disable/remove without waiting for repository loading.
1030	- **TRY** — dated scratch experiments, including non-Git folders, with durable
1031	  tags/notes and explicit active/deprecated/archived/graduated state.
1032	- **REMOTE** — repositories visible through authenticated forge CLIs, including
1033	  configured Azure DevOps projects, marked when a local repo or Try exists.
1034	  What can I open or clone.
1035	- **SKILLS** — native project/global agent-skill inventory for the exact startup
1036	  checkout plus global sources, with local presence/integrity and an explicitly
1037	  checked upstream freshness state. Outside Git it starts as a cross-repository
1038	  inventory over accepted REPOS targets; `A` toggles either launch context to all
1039	  accepted repositories for this TUI session.
1040	- **MCP** — sanitized static MCP declarations for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor,
1041	  Gemini CLI, and OpenCode, scoped to the same startup context by default and
1042	  sharing the `A` context/all toggle. It resolves only Claude's documented
1043	  project-approval settings; it does not claim connection health or a generally
1044	  effective merged runtime configuration.
1045	- **SSH** — canonical machines, exact SSH profiles, Tailscale/LAN observations and
1046	  fleet/Herdr membership. `r` reads local/cached state; `c` starts explicit discovery,
1047	  `n` opens setup, and `p` offers network or SSH tests for selected, machine,
1048	  or filtered profiles.
1049	
1050	The first view is constructed before runtime auto-detection, project-root lookup,
1051	cache decoding, shell-based tool checks, or the optional release refresh can
1052	finish. TASKS, REPOS, and TRY then publish independently from one shared local
1053	load cycle; REMOTE, SKILLS, MCP, and SSH remain lazy. FLEET warms missing/expired
1054	host snapshots after five seconds or an earlier visit, without blocking startup
1055	or prompting for authentication. A cached REMOTE/FLEET snapshot
1056	is immediately usable but is tracked separately from a current live result.
1057	Every requested view has its own generation, so `r` cancels the old read, a late
1058	result cannot replace a newer one, a failed refresh keeps usable rows visible,
1059	and a successful empty result clears obsolete rows. Warning-only SKILLS/MCP
1060	source diagnostics keep a fresh partial snapshot, and a visible dependent view
1061	resumes automatically after a failed REPOS generation is repaired and reloaded.
1062	
1063	TASKS, REPOS and TRY use the same services as their non-interactive commands.
1064	Git-backed Tries appear in TRY rather than being duplicated in REPOS; REMOTE
1065	still knows that local checkout exists. The repo list matters on day one: with
1066	forty repositories and no tasks recorded yet, a task-only dashboard would just
1067	be empty.
1068	
1069	Navigation is vim-style, arrows alongside:
1070	
1071	```
1072	j k        move                 ctrl+d ctrl+u   half a page
1073	g G        top / bottom         h l / tab       previous / next view

```text
6	# dev-cli
7	
8	Git owns code; a dev task records a branch-backed change stream. Work items may
9	span streams and agent sessions; runtimes remain host-local.

11	## Discover what you need
12	
13	Use leaf `--help` for syntax, `dev help <topic>` for workflows, and

19	## Preserve these boundaries
20	
21	- Opening needs no task. Select direct, branch or worktree deliberately; use
22	  explicit `--base`. Managed worktrees stay outside repositories.
23	- Task-free worktrees use `dev git worktree create/open`; cleanup stays reviewed.
24	  `dev repo list --json` supplies navigation candidates, not external preferences/history.
25	- Choose `dev work start` for recorded park/resume/retirement; it prepares
26	  checkout/runtime. Agent launch is explicit; parallel writers need disjoint ownership and verified targets.
27	- Completion, artifacts, retirement and branch deletion are separate. Finalize
28	  after writer exit; retire externally. Use `retire --base` when integration is unproven.
29	- Cached/unknown observations, runtime `done` and merged PRs never authorize
30	  cleanup. Resolve guards; never improvise force removal or bypass checks.
31	- `dev pr checkout <URL>` is task-free; `--try` creates an independent clone.
32	  Provisioning is explicit; merge never cleans up locally.
33	
34	## Read a reference for advanced operations
35	
36	- Worktrees/lifecycle: [ownership](references/worktree-ownership.md), [lifecycle](references/task-lifecycle.md).
37	- Agents/prompts: [agents](references/parallel-agents.md), [handoffs](references/prompt-handoffs.md).
38	- History retention, exact sessions and co-commit: [artifacts](references/ai-artifacts.md).
39	- Cleanup: [retirement](references/agent-retirement.md), [triage](references/local-triage.md).
40	- Hygiene/scans/redaction: [hygiene](references/hygiene.md).
41	- Forks/setup/organization: [setup](references/repository-bootstrap.md), [bootstrap](references/bootstrap.md).
42	- SSH/fleet: [SSH](references/ssh-hosts.md).

44	- Skill/MCP/instruction transfers, updates or removal: [transfers](references/agent-interop.md), [maintenance](references/skills-management.md).
45	- [Snippets](references/snippets.md).
46	- PR/MR pages, diffnav, gh-dash, checkout and merge: [pull requests](references/pull-requests.md).
47	- Recursive Git children: [submodules](references/submodules.md).
48	
49	## Unexpected dev failures
50	
51	Read [feedback and repair](references/feedback-and-repair.md). Preserve the
52	original task; extra investigation, repair, subagents and publication need
53	explicit consent covering scope and cost.
```

```text
1	# Command navigation
2	
3	`dev --help` presents 17 primary entrypoints. `dev help --tree` shows two levels
4	of the canonical tree; `--depth 0` expands all levels, an optional command path
5	focuses a subtree, and `--aliases` includes shortcuts. Use leaf `--help` for
6	syntax and `dev help <topic>` for workflow guidance.
7	
8	| Family | Operations |
9	|---|---|
10	| `work` | list/start/park/resume/done/adopt/retire/sweep |
11	| `repo` | repository operations, bootstrap, note, independent flow preview |
12	| `tries` | try/open/list/graduate/demote and retention |
13	| `git` | transactions, ignore, worktree, submodule, hygiene |
14	| `agent` | skill, mcp, instructions, prompt, artifact including prepare |
15	| `activity` | journal, durable stats |
16	| `self` | config/cache/doctor/version/upgrade/completion/shell-init/feedback |
17	
18	The independent roots are snippet, ssh, fleet, dotfile, pr, summary, triage,
19	status, tui and help. Older top-level spellings remain permanent shortcuts with
20	unchanged arguments, output and exit behavior. They do not emit deprecation
21	warnings. Existing JSON and task/catalog storage contracts are unchanged.
22	
23	`dev try <name>` and `dev tries try <name>` retain create-or-open semantics,
24	including names matching management verbs. `dev gist` retains GitHub-only scope.
25	`dev prepare` is `dev agent artifact prepare`; `dev edit` is `dev self config edit`.
26	`dev git ignore --stdout/--list` remains usable outside repositories.
27	
28	`dev repo cd <repo>` is equivalent to `dev repo open <repo> --runtime none`.
29	It preserves repository completion and resolution, always bypassing runtime
30	launch/focus. The shell wrapper consumes its directory handoff; without the
31	wrapper it prints a quoted `cd` command.
32	
33	Prefer canonical paths in new guidance. Root completion emphasizes these paths;
34	shortcut argument/flag completion stays available. Reload shell integration
35	after an upgrade with `dev self shell-init <shell>`.
36	
37	## Try graduation and demotion
38	
39	### Graduation (v0.3.1)
40	
41	`dev tries graduate [try]` and `dev graduate` share the terminal/dashboard
42	wizard: name, optional category, local (default)/add URL/create GitHub or GitLab,
43	then preview and confirm. The reviewed source identity and contents are
44	revalidated before apply. `--yes`/`-y` or non-TTY use runs directly from flags;
45	`--dry-run` never prompts, probes forge authentication, moves or publishes.
46	
47	Use `--remote-url` for an existing URL, or `--forge github|gitlab` for creation;
48	`--remote` retains automatic create-provider selection. Forge also accepts
```
